claims.reason: Backed: the abstract names task aversiveness, task delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness as strong predictors of procrastination, which supports looking for what hinders starting a task. Not backed: the part 'zamiast poprzestawać na samokrytyce' (the abstract says nothing about self-criticism) and any evidence that checking the obstacle changes whether a person starts; the review reports correlations only.

claims.reason: The grade letter B is editorial and was not checked. The words after it describe the source: a meta-analysis built on correlations, which reports predictors of procrastination (association) and, by design, is a review of possible causes and effects and not a trial of any intervention. The negative clause is read as a statement of design; an abstract cannot show that the full paper contains no intervention test.

The full text of Steel 2007 would be needed.

claims.reason: Supported in part: the abstract reports several different strong predictors and none of them is named as avoidance of unpleasant emotions or as lack of effort, so a single-cause reading does not follow from it. Not checkable from an abstract: whether the full paper makes any claim about emotion avoidance or effort; the full text would be needed.

scope_gaps.note: The title contrasts checking obstacles with self-criticism; the source is silent on self-criticism and does not test whether looking for the obstacle changes starting.
The advice lists 'niejasne' as an obstacle; the source snapshots name no such predictor.
No snapshot addresses small first steps or any intervention.
The abstract names 'task delay' without a definition; the item reads it as distance of the reward or the completion in time, which would have to be confirmed in the full text.

The sentence describes only the meta-analytic core. The abstract says the paper is also a theoretical review that draws on experimental and qualitative findings and presents temporal motivation theory; a reader might assume the whole paper is purely correlational.
The abstract does not describe which experimental findings the review used, so whether any measured an effect of a change in thinking is not visible.
Only the abstract was available; the full paper may discuss emotion regulation or effort in the text of the review.
